doc.title: Horn Shirley — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: What she heard in Garner's lyricism compared with Debussy
summary: Horn tries to explain the lyricism she found in both Garner and Debussy.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: What was it about Earl Garner‘s playing that really changed you? I mean, you cite him as the reason that you became a jazz musician, so what was it in his playing that you heard?

I hear . . . in the beginning I heard lyricism. I heard pretty stuff, and I heard, I heard, oh, good lord, what did I hear? I mean, I heard . . . man oh man oh man. Give me a minute now. I heard him willowing through trees, and I heard, oh god, I can‘t think.
When you say that you heard pretty stuff, you also have said that about Debussy.
How did Debussy‘s pretty things differ from Earl Garner‘s pretty things? You know, they‘re both beautiful. I‘m a big fan of both of theirs. But to your ears, how did
he differ? What was the difference that made one classical and one jazz, and made you want to go the way of jazz?

Well, with Debussy, you know, I studied him. I studied him. Dr. Hughes made me have that lyricism there, right, Debussy, right. Okay. Now, when you listen to Earl Garner, he‘s got all that lyricism there. I mean, he‘s just making all these kind of beautiful things, trees, and everything is just . . . I don‘t have it. I don‘t have it right. He just helped me. All the beauty and lyricism is right there. Oh, god, I can‘t . . . help me.
